name: come with a Motion or Sound Participial

entry.name: come with a Motion or Sound Participial

1.definition: Presents an approach with its manner or accompanying sound.
1.details: In came running, running supplies the manner. In came roaring past, roaring supplies sound during the movement and past supplies the path. The subject participates in the motion and the activity or sound. Compare came looking for us, where the participial can instead describe a purpose. This entry covers the manner and sound reading with come.

examples.form: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].
examples.note: Excerpt from the documented example. Running supplies manner.
Excerpt from a description of tanks. Roaring supplies the sound and past the path.

relatedConstructions.notes: Both the participial and any path expression are part of the motion description.
A goal expression can specify the destination of the movement.

grounds.note: Documents the motion frame and the distribution of manner and sound participles.

projection.target: A sound verb can describe how the movement unfolds, with a path expression that describes the movement rather than the direction of the sound.
projection.evidence: Patel’s Research Constructicon entry gives motion and sound examples. Fanego traces the corpus distribution of the broader movement-plus-participial pattern.

curious.title: Came running, came roaring
curious.summary: Come followed by an -ing word can show how someone approached or what sound came with the movement.
curious.body: In Sally came running excitedly into the room, running tells us how she arrived. In came roaring past, from a description of tanks, roaring is a sound heard during the movement, and past shows the path. The one who comes takes part in both the motion and the activity or sound. Compare came looking for us. There the -ing word can instead describe a purpose: they came in order to look for us.

examples.text: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].

curious.try: Say came running and then came looking for us. In which one does the -ing word tell how someone moved, and in which can it tell why they came?

teacher.summary: Helps students see come plus an -ing word as manner or sound of movement, and tell it apart from a purpose reading.
teacher.explain: In this pattern the head verb come is followed by a V-ing expression and optionally a path expression. In came running, running supplies the manner. In came roaring past, roaring supplies sound during the movement and past supplies the path; the path describes the movement, not the direction of the sound. The subject participates in the motion and in the activity or sound. A goal expression can also specify the destination. In came looking for us the participial can instead describe a purpose, a reading outside this pattern.
teacher.terms: V-ing form: the gerund-participial in CGEL, called the present participle in traditional grammar. Path and goal expressions are related to the goal complement entry.

examples.text: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].

contrasts.text: Sally came running into the room.

contrasts.note: The participial can describe a purpose instead.

watch_for: A learner might read came running as two separate events, coming and then running, when running describes how the coming happens.
A learner might read the -ing word as a purpose, as in came looking for us, when it supplies manner or sound.
A learner might take past in came roaring past as the direction of the sound, when it describes the movement.
teacher.activity: Students act out came running, came dancing and came looking for us. The class decides whether the -ing word tells how someone moved or why they came.

child.hook: What do you notice about the word after came in Sally came running into the room?
child.explain: You can add a word ending in -ing after came. It can tell how someone moved. Sally came running into the room.

examples.text: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].
The dog [came running into the kitchen].

child.play: Act out came running, came hopping and came skipping. Which word tells you how the person moved?
